sentences.text: France's distinctive role in the Allied Industrial Base is as its nuclear specialist and a broad, mid-sized equipment maker.
Allies rely on it for reactor parts, 20% of world exports or production, and it holds core seats in Nuclear Fuel & Reactor Systems and Electric Vehicles.
Elsewhere its roles are substitutable, and the AIB assigns it no primary strategic role at its current thresholds.
Its exposure is imported fuel and the control of imported equipment: oil and gas, grid and battery software, rare-earth magnets and transformer steel sit behind the High fence.
Its industrial effort should keep enrichment, wind parts and battery components competitive and catch up in EVs, drivetrains and battery cells, where allies also need new capacity.
Most of its manufacturing positions are a few percent of world supply, so catching up should go with allied makers.
The nuclear manufacturing calls need care, because their trade baskets mix reactor parts with boiler and steam-turbine parts.
At home only EV adoption needs a faster build-out, and France's own need gives its development cooperation a narrow base, battery cells.
Oil and gas supply, which takes one to three years to rebuild; potentially coercive suppliers provide 51% of oil imports.
The control software of battery, grid and inverter equipment.
Rare-earth magnets for EV motors, where China leads world rare-earth refining, and grain-oriented electrical steel for transformers.
The answer is trusted contracts, stocks, qualified suppliers and control of command paths, not self-sufficiency.
Preserve uranium enrichment, on 38% of world exports of enriched uranium, wind parts, and battery components.
Catch Up in EVs, EV drivetrain components and battery cells and packs, with allied makers where the base is thin.
Judge the nuclear parts and reactor Catch Up calls on reactor-specific measures.
Battery and EV minerals from trusted producers such as Canada, the United States and Australia; allied supply covers the need.
With developing partners, add trusted battery-cell capacity through development finance and offtake.
Accelerate EV adoption and charging, buying equipment competitively from trusted suppliers, with security conditions on connected equipment.
Leave open wafers and PV cells, polysilicon, plant equipment for gas, oil and coal, and uranium ore, bought from a diversified base of trusted producers.
Preserve and Catch Up fill the component and assembly columns of batteries, EVs, nuclear and wind, and enrichment is the only Preserve among the refining steps.
Secure sits only in oil and gas, Partner in the minerals France does not mine, and deployment is mostly Watch.
Orange corner flags mark High-fence parts inside other steps: control software, EV magnets and transformer steel.
Violet flags mark Catch Up layers inside Watch steps, such as solar cells and polysilicon, which inherit their steps' anchors.
Each cell is a supply-chain step of a technology, colored by its strategic choice.
A corner flag marks a mixed step whose named parts sit behind a different fence: in battery cells and packs, the battery software is Secure, the cells Catch Up and the enclosures Watch.
A dotted outline marks a review case, a call resting on low confidence, a review flag, a thin anchor or a known data artifact; this brief does not turn those calls into recommendations.
lack the data for a call.
Secure covers two whole steps and eight layers inside other steps, grouped into five capabilities, all in the table with oil and gas together.
Secure means surviving a prolonged cutoff or a hostile command through trusted supply, stocks, redundancy or control of the command path, not making everything at home.
Need is 98 for oil and 91 for gas out of a hundred, and rebuilding supply takes one to three years.
Potentially coercive suppliers provide 51% of oil and 25% of gas imports; allied supply falls short for oil.
Stocks sized to the rebuild time; capacity reservations with trusted producers such as Canada, Norway and the United States.
Control software of grids, inverters and batteries
Firmware and grid-control software can command equipment from abroad.
China supplies 51% of battery and 25% of PV and inverter imports: hardware shares, not software.
Trusted-source and certification rules for firmware and remote access; a replacement program for the installed base.
The core steel of power transformers.
The call rests on its step, grid metals refining: need 73, trusted suppliers 5% of world supply, a figure unrelated steps repeat; potentially coercive suppliers provide only 6% of its imports.
Capacity reservations with trusted steelmakers; spares pools for transformers.
They drive the traction motors of France's EVs.
China holds 94% of rare-earth and battery-metal refining, a step-wide share that battery materials repeats; trusted suppliers 4%; rebuilding takes more than three years.
Offtake and allied agreements; stockpiles; adversary-source limits, phased in as trusted supply qualifies.
Turbine, vehicle, reactor and oil and gas network controls read Watch for France.
Inside blades, towers and nacelle parts, the same magnets read Preserve on that step's position, not on magnet output.
Medium fence — where industrial capability matters
This is where France makes its real industrial choices: is a capability worth having (Strategic Industrial Value), and how strong is France today (Competitive Position)?
Most French positions rest on world supply shares of a few percent, ranking high only among the economies that already make them.
Uranium conversion and enrichment reads Preserve on a position of 95.
Its measured anchor is exports of enriched uranium, 38% of the world's.
Its supply share of 25% counts uranium compounds, yellowcake included, and converted uranium trades under the mining step's codes, so the data see enrichment, not conversion.
With Russia holding 22% of that compound-based supply, trusted enrichment matters to allies.

Wind turbines (90) and blades, towers and nacelle parts (83) rest on operating capacity, but on 2% of world supply each, and the turbine step's trade codes are mostly cables, transformers and switchgear.
Battery components (82) rest on three anchors with moderate confidence.
PV modules and inverters read Preserve only on low confidence, a review case.
EV and charger manufacturing (62) and EV drivetrain components (54) combine high value with high confidence; vehicles rest on three anchors, operating capacity among them.
Battery cells and packs add high need (79) but rest on a single anchor, 1% of world supply, while China provides 51% of imports.
Nuclear fuel and reactor parts (71) and reactors and steam generators (37) also read Catch Up, but their trade baskets mix reactor parts with generic boiler and steam-turbine parts.
The AIB's own measure, 20% of world exports or production of reactor parts, is the firmer sign of a nuclear supplier.
Other Catch Up calls are weaker than they look, and this brief does not build on them:
Battery materials and rare-earth refining: both at a position of 0, each on a single export share (2% and 1%).
Both show China with 94% of world supply, an identical share that suggests overlapping trade codes.
Battery recycling: a single export share (3%) in trade codes for battery waste, scrap and residues.
Rare-earth and wind materials refining: low confidence, a review case.

France holds 0% of world supply in battery and EV minerals and no pathway to scale it, so it should depend deliberately on trusted producers such as Canada, the United States and Australia; allied supply covers the need.
Its largest supplier today, Gabon, is outside that list.
Waste-oil recovery reads Partner on low confidence, a review case.
Some capabilities sit in several technology chains with different calls; the table keeps the national reading apart from what allies rely on France for.

Each technology is split into supply-chain stages from extraction to recycling, and each step gets a strategic choice by fixed rules applied in order:
Secure where an acute vulnerability is measured;
at deployment, Accelerate where deployment need reaches 60;
Watch where the step is a large, commoditized yard;
Preserve where Competitive Position is in the top quarter (75) and either Strategic Industrial Value (bar 60) or supply-chain need (bar 67) is high;
Catch Up where the value is high, the position is not, and a capability anchor is corroborated by other evidence;
Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;
Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed.
A value that rests on market size alone is capped just under the bar.
Observed policy never decides a choice.

The high fence (Secure) protects what cannot be allowed to fail; the medium fence covers capabilities worth building, keeping or sourcing deliberately and deployment to accelerate; the low fence (Watch) leaves a step open to competitive purchase.
Some calls rest on low confidence, an engine review flag, a thin capability anchor, a known data artifact or, at deployment, a single indicator of low confidence.
They stay on the map but never enter the Bottom line, the Agenda, the policy table or a headline mark.
